procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated as Writ Petitions (Criminal) Nos. 205 & 206 of 2018 before the Supreme Court itself.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The order challenged was the potential hearing of the writ petitions by the Hon’ble Bench comprising Hon’ble Mr. Justice Madan B. Lokur and Hon’ble Mr Justice Uday Umesh Lalit. The applicants sought their recusal.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings mentioned in the text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the applicants/petitioners filed interlocutory applications (Crl.M.P. No. 125554 of 2018 and Crl.M.P. No. 125550 of 2018) within the existing Writ Petitions (Criminal) Nos. 205 & 206 of 2018, specifically requesting the recusal of the designated bench. The Supreme Court considered these applications for recusal but found no merit in them and dismissed them. The Court then directed that the writ petitions be listed for preliminary hearing on 26th November, 2018.

issue.issue_text: Whether the interlocutory applications for recusal of the judges should be allowed.

facts: Applicants filed interlocutory applications requesting that the two judges on the Bench recuse themselves from hearing the writ petitions.

The basis for the recusal request was that observations made by the Court on a previous date (July 30, 2018) created a "real apprehension" that the ongoing investigations or any subsequent trial would be prejudiced against the applicants.
The applicants wanted the case to be placed before a different Bench for monitoring.
law: Once an investigation is complete and a charge sheet is filed, the trial court is in "complete charge and full control of the proceedings."
Constitutional courts typically keep their "hands off" the matter after a charge sheet is filed to avoid interfering with the due course of justice.
Professional investigative bodies are expected to conduct their work independently and not be swayed by observations made by a court during the monitoring process.
application: The Court rejected the argument that its prior observations would influence a future trial. It reasoned that any trial judge would act with fairness and independence, and to suggest otherwise was to question the integrity of the judiciary.

The Court also dismissed the concern that its observations would impact the Special Investigation Team (SIT), stating its confidence that the SIT consists of professionals who would not be swayed by judicial remarks.

The Court noted arguments from the Amicus Curiae that the applications were an attempt at "forum shopping" and that allowing recusal based on a judge's probing questions would set a dangerous precedent.
Ultimately, the Court found no basis for the applicants' apprehensions and determined that the applications lacked merit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the applications for recusal, finding no merit in the claim that its prior observations would prejudice the investigation or a potential trial. The Court affirmed the independence of both the trial courts and the investigating team and accordingly dismissed the applications.

issue.issue_text: Whether observations made by the Supreme Court would improperly influence the investigation by the Special Investigation Team (SIT) or interfere with the due judicial process.

facts: The applicants/petitioners expressed an apprehension that observations made by the Supreme Court on July 30, 2018, would improperly influence the investigation by the Special Investigation Team (SIT) and the subsequent judicial process.
No allegations of unfairness, lack of impartiality, or lack of integrity have been made against the SIT.
Similarly, no allegations have been made suggesting that any Trial Judge has shown a lack of independence.
law: Courts generally cannot interfere in investigations, and no interference in the judicial process is permissible.
An exception to non-interference in investigations may occur in rare cases of unjustified deviation or illegal interference, which is why Constitutional Courts sometimes monitor investigations.
Once a final report or charge sheet is filed, the concerned trial court is in complete charge and full control of the proceedings, and Constitutional Courts keep their hands off the matter.
application: The Court found no basis for the apprehension that its observations would impact the SIT's decisions.
It reasoned that the SIT is an independent body composed of professionals who would not be swayed by any observations made by a court during a continuing mandamus process.
The Court also dismissed the fear of interference in the judicial process, stating that once a charge sheet is filed, the trial court has full control.
It held that harboring such an apprehension was inappropriate as it indirectly and unwittingly questioned the fairness and independence of the judiciary.
The Court concluded that the petitioners' apprehension was neither real nor justified.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' contention, finding their apprehension that the Court's observations would influence the SIT or interfere with the judicial process to be erroneous and unjustified. The Court affirmed the independence and professionalism of both the SIT and the judiciary, stating they would not be swayed by its remarks. To remove any doubt, the Court explicitly clarified that its observations were not intended to compromise the integrity or fairness of the SIT or the concerned judges.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the interlocutory applications for recusal of the judges should be allowed.
appellant_arguments: Submissions were made in interlocutory applications for the recusal of the judges. (The text does not specify the content of these submissions).
respondent_arguments: The learned Attorney General appearing on behalf of the Union of India supported the prayer made in the applications for recusal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether observations made by the Supreme Court would improperly influence the investigation by the Special Investigation Team (SIT) or interfere with the due judicial process.
appellant_arguments: The Attorney General, on behalf of the Union of India, argued that the observations made by the Court had a demoralizing effect on the Indian Army, the paramilitary forces, and the Manipur Police, affecting their morale in the fight against insurgency.
respondent_arguments: The observations made by this Court had a demoralising effect on the Indian Army, the paramilitary forces and the Manipur Police or in any event, it had affected the morale of these forces in their fight against insurgency.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is not that every single allegation must necessarily be inquired into, particularly when the allegations are very general in nature and no substantive steps have been taken by the complainant, such as lodging a first information report (FIR) or filing a writ petition.
obiter: It must be remembered that we are not dealing with individual cases but a systemic or institutional response relating to constitutional criminal law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the apprehension of the applicants that justice would not be done to them due to the court's prior observations was misplaced, if not unfounded. The court reasoned that there can be no interference in investigations or the judicial process, except in rare cases of unjustified deviation. Since this was not such a case, the apprehension that the court's observations would lead to interference in the SIT investigation or the due judicial process was not real or justified.
legal_tests_applied: The general rule is that there can be no interference in investigations and the courts cannot brook any interference in the judicial process.

An exception to the general rule against non-interference occurs when there is an unjustified deviation from the natural course of investigations or illegal interference in the judicial process, which is a rare situation to be dealt with on a case-by-case basis.
why_appellant_lost: The court held that the applicants' apprehension that justice will not be done to them is misplaced if not unfounded.
The court found that the apprehension that its observations would cause interference in the investigations by the SIT or in the due judicial process was not real or justified.
The applicants did not cast any doubt on the integrity and fairness of the investigations being conducted by the SIT.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the principle that courts do not interfere in investigations except in extraordinary circumstances, which were not present here.
The court determined that the applicants' fear of a tainted investigation or trial was not a real or justified basis for recusal or for halting the ongoing proceedings.
policy_considerations: Constitutional Courts monitor investigations on extraordinary occasions to pre-empt an unjustified deviation from the natural course of investigations or illegal interference in the judicial process.
